title: Seasonal transition dates can reveal biases in Arctic sea ice simulations
abstract: Abstract. Arctic sea ice experiences a dramatic annual cycle, and seasonal ice loss and growth can be characterized by various metrics: melt onset, breakup, opening, freeze onset, freeze-up, and closing. By evaluating a range of seasonal sea ice metrics, CMIP6 sea ice simulations can be evaluated in more detail than by using traditional metrics alone, such as sea ice area. We show that models capture the observed asymmetry in seasonal sea ice transitions, with spring ice loss taking about 1–2 months longer than fall ice growth. The largest impacts of internal variability are seen in the inflow regions for melt and freeze onset dates, but all metrics show pan-Arctic model spreads exceeding the internal variability range, indicating the contribution of model differences. Through climate model evaluation in the context of both observations and internal variability, we show that biases in seasonal transition dates can compensate for other unrealistic aspects of simulated sea ice. In some models, this leads to September sea ice areas in agreement with observations for the wrong reasons.
field: Evaluation of Arctic sea ice simulations
problem: Traditional evaluation of sea ice in climate models using metrics like sea ice area can obscure underlying process biases, leading to models that seem accurate for the wrong reasons and contributing to large projection uncertainty.
method: This study proposes using a range of seasonal sea ice transition dates, such as melt onset and freeze-up, to evaluate climate models and reveal biases in Arctic sea ice simulations that are obscured when using traditional metrics like sea ice area.
task: The task is to assess biases in CMIP6 Arctic sea ice simulations by evaluating a range of seasonal transition metrics, such as melt onset and freeze-up, against observational data and considering the role of internal variability.

This dataset includes seasonal sea ice indicators from 1 March 1979 through 27 February 2017, derived from sea ice concentration data from the NOAA/NSIDC Climate Data Record of Passive Microwave Sea Ice Concentration and brightness temperature observations from the DMSP SSM/I-SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Brightness Temperatures.

This dataset includes seasonal sea ice indicators from 1 March 1979 through 27 February 2017, derived from sea ice concentration data from the NOAA/NSIDC Climate Data Record of Passive Microwave Sea Ice Concentration and brightness temperature observations from the DMSP SSM/I-SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Brightness Temperatures.

In satellite retrievals, continuous melt and freeze onset are defined using the brightness temperature of the surface because brightness temperature is sensitive to the phase of water (Markus et al., 2009; Steele et al., 2019). Brightness temperatures are collected at the 19V and 37V polarizations from SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS sensors.
